body.objective: Students will be able to identify my values.
successCriteria: I can identify my values and where they come from
I can explain how values guide decisions
I can discuss a dilemma respectfully
body.hook: You find a $20 bill on the hallway floor. Nobody saw you. What do you do? Most people answer quickly, but if you ask them why, the answers get interesting. Some say "because it's the rule," some say "because I'd want it back," and some say "because of the kind of person I want to be." Those reasons come from values.

vocabulary.definition: A belief about what is important or right.
Thinking carefully about what is right and wrong and why.
A situation where you must choose between options that each have good and bad points.
A rule or belief that guides behaviour, such as honesty.
A particular way of seeing a situation.

study.title: What Matters to Me?
study.question: What are my values, and how do they guide my choices?
study.passage:
Part 1, Values sort (10 minutes): Each student gets 20 value cards: honesty, kindness, fairness, loyalty, courage, responsibility, respect, family, friendship, freedom, achievement, faith or spirituality, creativity, health, fun, security, generosity, independence, justice, the environment. Sort them into "very important," "important" and "less important." Choose your top five.
Part 2, Where do values come from? (5 minutes): Families, cultures, faith communities, friends, teachers, experiences and media. Values can change as we grow.
Part 3, Values in action (15 minutes): Discuss these dilemmas in small groups. For each, name which values are in conflict.
A. Your best friend asks you to say they were with you on Saturday so they won't get in trouble at home. (loyalty vs honesty)
B. You see a classmate copying answers during a test. (fairness vs friendship)
C. Your team could win the championship if you play while slightly injured, against the coach's advice. (achievement vs health and responsibility)
Part 4, Discussion norms: Listen fully. Question ideas, not people. Give reasons. It's okay to change your mind.
There is not always one right answer, but some reasons are stronger than others.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Sort the value cards and choose your top five
Analyze three dilemmas for conflicting values
Reflect on how values guide your decisions
organizer: What I would do and why
discussion: Which of your top five values was hardest to choose?
In Dilemma A, which value would you choose, and why?
Did anyone in your group see a dilemma differently? How?
Can two good values conflict? Give an example.
study.product: Write a reflection on your top three values: where each comes from, a time it guided a decision, and a dilemma where two of your values might conflict.

body.objective: Students will be able to use ethical lenses.
successCriteria: I can describe five ethical lenses
I can apply each lens to a dilemma
I can explain why lenses sometimes disagree
body.hook: Two people can look at the same situation and reach different answers about what's right, not because one is careless, but because they're looking through different "lenses." Learning the main ethical lenses helps you see a problem from every angle.

vocabulary.definition: A way of looking at a moral question that focuses on one kind of consideration.
Choosing the action that produces the most good and least harm for everyone affected.
Choosing the action that respects people's rights and keeps our duties and promises.
Choosing the action that treats people equally or fairly.
Choosing the action a person of good character would take.
Choosing the action that best protects relationships and responds to people's needs.

study.title: Looking Through Lenses
study.question: How do different ethical lenses help us reason about right and wrong?
study.passage:
The five lenses (written for this lesson; a common framework in ethics education):
1. Consequences: Which option produces the most good and least harm for everyone affected?
2. Rights and duties: Which option respects everyone's rights and keeps promises and responsibilities, even if the outcome isn't the best?
3. Fairness: Which option treats people equally, or fairly given their situation?
4. Virtue: Which option shows the kind of person I want to be: honest, brave, kind, responsible?
5. Care: Which option best protects relationships and meets the needs of people who depend on me?
Dilemma (fictional): Maya promised to keep her friend Sam's secret. Sam tells her he has been skipping meals to save money for a school trip and feels dizzy in class. Should Maya tell an adult?
Activity: groups each take one lens, decide what it suggests, then report. Discuss where the lenses agree and where they pull apart. Which lens felt most convincing, and why?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; the lenses summarize widely taught approaches in ethics.
discussion: Which lenses pulled in different directions?
Why might the rights and duties lens focus on the promise?
Which lens do you tend to use most?
study.product: Apply all five lenses to a dilemma of your choice and write which action you'd choose and why.

body.objective: Students will be able to apply a decision-making model to a dilemma.
body.iCan: I can apply a decision-making model to a dilemma.
successCriteria: I can follow a step-by-step ethical decision-making model
I can identify facts, stakeholders and options
I can justify a decision and reflect on it
body.hook: When a hard choice comes up, it's tempting to go with your first feeling. A decision-making model slows you down just enough to see the facts, the people affected and your real options, so you choose something you can stand behind.

vocabulary.definition: A step-by-step process for making careful choices.
A situation where every choice has a downside or where values conflict.
Thinking back on a decision to learn from it.

study.title: Deciding Well
study.question: How can a step-by-step model help me make ethical decisions?
study.passage:
The STOP-THINK-ACT model (written for this lesson):
1. Stop and recognize: Is this an ethical issue? What values are in conflict?
2. Get the facts: What do I know? What don't I know? Who can I ask?
3. Identify stakeholders: Who is affected, and how?
4. List options: at least three, including creative ones.
5. Test options with the lenses: consequences, rights and duties, fairness, virtue, care. Also try quick tests: Would I be comfortable if my decision were shared publicly? What would someone I admire do?
6. Decide and act.
7. Reflect: How did it turn out? What would I do differently?
Dilemma (fictional): Jordan sees a group chat where classmates are planning to share an embarrassing edited photo of another student. Jordan's best friend is in the chat. What should Jordan do?
Groups work through all seven steps, then compare decisions and reasons.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: Which option passed the most tests?
How did using a model change your first reaction?
study.product: Work through the seven-step model on a dilemma and write a justified decision with a reflection.
